name: PT Pertamina Geothermal Energy Tbk

frontmatter.title: Pertamina Geothermal Energy: a contracted baseload yield priced for a stalled build
frontmatter.summary: PGEO sells steam and electricity to PLN under long take-or-pay contracts from operating geothermal fields with high availability. The shares trade below the DCF value of the contracted fleet because the market discounts a capital-hungry growth plan. We rate BUY on the DCF alone: the cash yield is a fraction of a point below the sovereign and the dividend yield below it too, so the income case is not made and we do not claim it.
thesis: Contracted baseload: revenue comes from PLN take-or-pay steam and electricity contracts [S3], availability runs near 98.5% [S5] and the fuel is free, so EBITDA is an annuity rather than a commodity bet.

The data pack understates the business: it carries depreciation of 126.9 against the audited charge inside cost of revenue [S3]. On restated numbers FY2025 EBITDA is 332.5 and the shares trade on 5.5x EV/EBITDA, not the multiple the raw feed implies.

The build is the swing factor, not the tariff: adding capacity from 727 MW towards the company target needs capital at returns close to our cost of capital [S4,S5], so growth is close to value-neutral and scepticism about the gigawatt-scale story is fair.

What we disagree with is the price, not the plan: the reverse DCF says the market discounts revenue growth of about 0.7% a year from FY2027E on our own cash flows, below what the capacity we have already commissioned delivers.

The income case does not carry the rating: on a consistent period the AFFO yield sits a fraction of a point below the ten-year sovereign, and the dividend yield of 7.1% — on a payout of 89.9% of FY2025 earnings [S2] — is below it too. We rate the shares on the DCF, not on the yield [S0].

blocks.text: We initiate on Pertamina Geothermal Energy with a BUY rating and a target price of Rp1,395 against a last price of Rp930, an expected total return of 57.0% [S0]. The company owns and operates geothermal working areas in Indonesia and sells steam and electricity to PLN under long-dated take-or-pay contracts; it produces at a capacity factor of 89.9% against a global industry average in the high seventies [S4], and its fuel costs nothing. Revenue is closer to an annuity than to a commodity exposure, which is the property we are paying for.

The variant view is not that PGEO will hit its growth targets. It is that the market prices the company as though the growth plan consumes all the cash and produces nothing, when the existing fleet alone supports a value above the current price. Our reverse DCF shows the market discounting revenue growth of roughly 0.7% a year from FY2027E on the same model — below the long-run inflation rate, not merely a slower build — while the contracted assets deliver a high-single-digit revenue increase this year on capacity already commissioned: the first nine months of 2026 produced 4,114 GWh and company-reported EBITDA of 288 USD m on figures published in November [S5]. We model FY2026E revenue of 471.7 and EBITDA of 382.4.

A target this far above the price is a claim about the market rather than about our optimism. The base-case DCF alone is worth well above the last price, on a 8.8% cost of capital and a terminal value that is under a third of the enterprise value; the shares have fallen with an index that lost more than two-fifths of its value between the end of 2025 and early November [S10], and nothing in the audited accounts or the November operating release explains a discount of that size [S3,S5]. We should say plainly what the rating does not rest on: the method card's cash-yield hurdle is not met. On a consistent period the AFFO yield is a fraction of a point below the ten-year rupiah sovereign of 7.4%, and the dividend yield of 7.1% is below it too, so the BUY is a discounted-cash-flow call and the valuation section sets out the arithmetic rather than claiming a spread we do not have.

What moves the value, in order of importance. First, capital intensity: the build absorbs 184.6 in FY2027E and 185.0 in FY2028E, 38.0% and 34.0% of revenue, and an overrun of a fifth on that path is in the bear case — which is why the valuation section spends most of its space on the capex build-up rather than the tariff. Second, the tariff regime: the PPAs sit under Perpres 112/2022 and management is lobbying for a revision [S4]; an upward revision is genuine upside we do not capitalise. Third, the 2028 green bond: it is fixed at its coupon to maturity [S3] and the group holds 714 USD m of cash against it [S5], so we treat refinancing at a higher rate as a risk rather than a base-case cost.

We are deliberately not paying for the full growth target, in either direction. The company plans 1,047 MW of installed capacity in 2028 and more than double that within the following decade [S4,S5], from 727 MW today [S5]. At the Hululais benchmark of 435 USD m for 110 MW [S4], that programme absorbs cash at a rate the balance sheet can fund but the equity should not pay a premium for: we estimate the return on new capital lands close to our cost of capital of 8.8%. Growth that earns its cost of capital is worth book value, not a multiple of it. The symmetry matters for the valuation: the 1,800 MW ambition is excluded from the revenue path in every scenario, so its capex is charged in none of them; the bull carries only faster delivery of the twelve priority projects and the tariff revision. The brownfield unit-cost saving [S5] is a qualitative upside we do not capitalise, because a permanent capex cut would also cut terminal replacement capex below depreciation and shrink the asset base.

Geothermal is the one renewable technology in Indonesia that behaves like baseload plant: the steam comes out of the ground whether or not the sun shines or the wind blows, so the operator sells capacity as well as energy. That is why a resource base among the largest anywhere has attracted state capital rather than merchant developers: the economics work only under long contracts with a creditworthy buyer.

PGEO develops and operates geothermal working areas and sells the output to PLN. The audited accounts describe two segments: own operations, where the company manages the fields at Sibayak, Kamojang, Lahendong, Ulubelu, Karaha and Lumut Balai, and joint operating contracts, where it earns a margin over fields operated with partners under contracts running to the middle of the century [S3]. FY2025 revenue was 432.7, of which 415 USD m was the subtotal of steam and electricity sales — all of it to PLN and its subsidiary PLN Indonesia Power, both related parties [S3] — and the remainder was production allowances from third parties [S3].

The contract architecture is the business model. Steam is sold under Steam Sales Contracts and electricity under Energy Sales Contracts; the Kamojang contracts apply take-or-pay, the electricity contracts apply take-or-pay, and the company carries delivery-or-pay obligations where it fails to supply the contracted minimum [S3]. Terms are long: Kamojang runs to 2040, the Lahendong steam contract runs thirty years from the last unit's commercial operation, Ulubelu to 2041, and the Lumut Balai and Hululais contracts run thirty years from the commercial operation of their final units [S3]. Revenue is therefore capacity-driven rather than volume-driven, and the operator is paid for being available.

Capacity and output. The company operates 727 MW of installed capacity in its own operations [S5] and produced 4,114 GWh in the first nine months of 2026, a record, with revenue growing at a double-digit rate over the same period [S4,S5]. Availability was 98.5% with a forced outage rate close to zero [S5]. The newest unit, Lumut Balai's second, obtained its operating certificate on 29 June 2025 with 55.0 MW [S3], which is why current revenue is growing faster than the fleet.

Ownership and group. PGEO is controlled by PT Pertamina Power Indonesia within the state-owned Pertamina group; the free float is 11.2% and the balance is held by the Pertamina group [S4]. Two consequences follow. The company is a strategic vehicle for the state's geothermal ambitions as much as a listed company, and its liquidity is thin enough that management has committed to raising the free float to 12.5% in March 2027 and 15.0% in 2028 through a divestment or a new share issue, while ruling out a buyback precisely because it would shrink the float [S4].

Strategy. Management describes three layers: optimise the operating fields, accelerate twelve priority projects that add 320 MW towards the growth target, and develop a longer pipeline including a project that already holds a signed power purchase agreement for the end of the decade [S5]. There is also a Beyond Electricity strategy whose most visible piece is a pilot to supply baseload geothermal power to a green data centre at Kamojang [S7]. That is a demand-side option rather than a revenue line today, but it is the most credible answer to who buys incremental geothermal output if PLN's own build is slow. We carry it at zero in the base case: no tariff, volume or contract has been published, so there is nothing to value, and it appears only in the bull case as one route to growth above the regulated ceiling.

Indonesia's geothermal resource is an order of magnitude larger than what the country has installed, which the industry puts at a small fraction of the national potential [S5,S8]. PLN's 2025-2034 business plan targets 5,200 MW of geothermal capacity by 2034, more than doubling the installed base, and PLN's own commercial director describes collaboration with Pertamina as crucial to getting there [S8]. PGEO is the largest listed geothermal operator in the country and the state's principal vehicle for that build, which is both its moat and its constraint.

The regulatory framework is the binding constraint. Tariffs for new and renewable generation sit under Perpres 112/2022, and PGEO's chief executive is publicly asking for the scheme to be revised so that geothermal investment carries a return that attracts capital without overburdening the state budget [S4]. He repeats the ask in the data-centre context: tariffs should be more competitive, more transparent and more predictable, fiscal incentives and green financing should be widened, and working areas, the PLN plan, the grid, the PPAs and commercial operation dates need to be synchronised [S7]. Read plainly, the company is telling you the current ceiling does not clear its hurdle rate on new projects. That is why we treat the growth plan as value-neutral and the tariff revision as the main upside option.

Competitive position and five forces. The buyer side is a single counterparty, PLN, which is both why the revenue is bankable and why pricing power sits with the government rather than with PGEO [S3]. Supplier power is low: the fuel is free and the main inputs are drilling contractors and turbines. New entrants are constrained by the resource, by permits and by the same tariff; the 2026 public expose lists partners and joint operating contracts across several fields [S3,S5]. Substitutes exist in the sense that PLN can build coal, gas or solar instead, and the relative cost of geothermal is exactly what the tariff review is about. Rivalry among geothermal operators is muted because the constraint is capital and permits rather than market share. The structure is unattractive on pricing and attractive on volume and contract length: a regulated utility with a state monopsonist.

Our moat assessment is narrow and contractual. The fields are irreplaceable and the take-or-pay contracts protect the installed base's cash flow until the power purchase agreements run off [S3]. But the moat does not extend to new capacity: each new megawatt must be justified at the regulated tariff, so growth is not automatically worth a premium. The house method card's framing for regulated infrastructure applies: model this as a bond with growth options, not as a compounder.

External influences. Three matter. The first is the rate path and the currency: the company reports in US dollars with rupiah-denominated shares, so the equity carries Indonesian risk premia and translation even though revenue is dollar-linked [S0,S3]. The second is Indonesian electricity demand, which PLN expects to rise sharply as the government debates a very large capacity increase over the next decade [S8]. The third is the domestic equity market: the composite index fell by more than forty percent between the end of 2025 and early November 2026, a drawdown the chief executive explicitly said had not changed the company's fundamentals [S10]. A market that falls that far reprices good and bad assets alike, which is part of why a contracted utility is available at a discount.

Revenue. FY2025 revenue was 432.7, up from 407.1 [S3], a modest year because Lumut Balai's second unit only started operating in the second half. The first nine months of 2026 grew revenue by 10.5% year on year with net profit up by a fifth and EBITDA of 288 USD m [S4,S5]. We forecast FY2026E revenue of 471.7 and then 485.8, 544.1, 587.6 and 611.2 through FY2030E. The path is the capacity bridge, not a tariff assumption: the FY2026E growth rate of 9.0% is below the nine-month rate only because the fourth quarter of 2025 already contained a full quarter of Lumut Balai's second unit, so the comparison base is high; FY2027E growth of 3.0% is the remaining annualisation of that unit plus the first binary units with 2027 target COD [S5], and the LK's PPA note discloses no escalator [S3], so we add none. FY2028E and FY2029E at 12.0% and 8.0% phase Hululais and the twelve priority projects rather than assuming the 2028 capacity target lands in full: Hululais was 87.8% complete at the end of 2025 with commercial operation still estimated for 2028 [S3], and its shareholders' agreement and power purchase agreement were still being finalised at the November 2026 public expose [S5].

Margins and costs. The cost of revenue is dominated by depreciation: 126.9 of 199.7 in FY2025 [S3]. That is the single most important restatement in this report. The data pack carries a depreciation charge of about one million dollars for the same year because it reads a direct-method cash flow statement that does not show depreciation as an add-back [S0,S3]. Every EBITDA, EV/EBITDA and leverage figure computed off the raw feed is therefore wrong by a third of the cost base. On the audited numbers FY2025 EBITDA was 332.5 at a margin of 76.8%, and the first nine months of 2026 ran above that [S5]. We hold the gross margin at the derived 9M2026 run-rate of 57.9%, so cash costs grow with revenue and there is no further margin assumption after FY2026E. The EBITDA margin nevertheless rises from 76.8% in FY2025A to 81.1% in FY2026E, and we want that expansion explicit rather than incidental: it is Lumut Balai's second unit running a full year against a largely fixed cost base, which lifts the gross margin to the derived level from the audited 53.9%, plus the 15.0% year-on-year fall in general and administrative expense in 9M2026 [S4], which carries into our FY2026E level of 26.9 (5.7% of revenue) against 30.7 in FY2025. The resulting margin sits about four points above the FY2025 actual; that is the model's calibration gap, it is sourced to those two items, and it is disclosed here rather than smoothed away.

Cash flow and capital allocation. Audited operating cash flow was 314 USD m in FY2025 against capex of 84.4 and dividends paid of 136.4 [S3], so the business funded its build and its distribution and still added cash that year. Free cash flow to the firm — after tax, working capital and capex, before financing — was 184.1 on the same audited numbers [S3], the figure the DCF discounts. The company declared 124 USD m on FY2025 earnings at a payout ratio of 89.9% [S2], above the fifty percent ceiling in the prospectus, which it can pass with shareholder approval and has done repeatedly [S2]. We hold the payout at 89.9% for FY2026E because the company has reopened a distribution above half of earnings for the year [S2] and the cover shown above survives our capex path; the payout is not a fixed policy, and a capex overrun that breaks the cover is the bear case's dividend channel.

Balance sheet and debt. The 30 September 2026 interim reports 714 USD m of cash and 956 USD m of total liabilities but no debt split [S5]; the last audited balance sheet, at 31 December 2025, carries gross debt of 752.9 — the green bond of 400 USD m due in April 2028, bank loans, current maturities and leases [S3]. The valuation is therefore struck on the 30 September 2026 balance sheet, with net debt of about thirty-five million dollars from the data pack [S0] — within a million dollars of the audited year-end figure of 34.4 [S3], so the date changes nothing in the value but the label is the model's date, not the audit's. Net debt is 0.1 turns of EBITDA [S3], low for infrastructure and the reason the equity is not a leveraged rate bet. The refinancing wall is that 2028 bond. Two debt costs appear in this report and the difference is deliberate: the P&L carries interest at 4.5%, in line with the effective rate the FY2025 accounts imply (30.3 of finance cost on opening debt of 745.8 [S3]) and the fixed coupon on the green bond [S3]; the WACC, set out below, uses the forward marginal cost of a new US dollar borrowing. The company need not pay that marginal rate: 30 September 2026 cash of 714 USD m against FY2025 audited gross debt of 752.9 [S3,S5] is enough to retire that bond at maturity. Self-funding saves the spread between the green-bond coupon and the 4.3% the cash earns today, which is a real but small number — a fraction of a percent of equity value — and it is the reason we treat the 2028 refinancing as a risk rather than a cost that must be paid.

Earnings quality. We ran the house screens. The accruals ratio is not a concern: operating cash flow exceeds net profit and the gap is depreciation rather than working capital. Receivables are almost entirely from PLN group entities [S3], a credit concentration rather than a collection problem, and they are flat year on year against growing revenue. The related-party channel is the whole revenue line, not a slice of it: 415 USD m of steam and electricity sales went to PLN group companies at regulated prices [S3], which is a concentration to underwrite but not a value-transfer mechanism. We found no special-monitoring board status or notation letter attaching to the shares and no pledge of the controlling stake [S3]. There is no evidence of capitalised development costs flattering the P&L: assets under construction are disclosed project by project, including Hululais at 87.8% complete [S3]. The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, a member firm of Ernst & Young, with an unmodified opinion [S3]. We flag one optics-class item: the dividend has been paid above the prospectus ceiling for two years, legal with shareholder approval but evidence that the controlling shareholder sets distribution policy [S2].

We value PGEO principally on discounted free cash flow to the firm, with an EV/EBITDA cross-check and a dividend-yield cross-check at low weight. The method fits because the assets produce contracted, dollar-linked cash flow against a known capital programme: what matters is the level and timing of capex against contracted revenue, not a commodity price. The house method card for regulated infrastructure makes the same point and adds the AFFO test, which we run below.

Our WACC is 8.8%, built as 4.9% + 0.76 × (4.2% + 2.5%) = 10.0% for the cost of equity — the US dollar risk-free rate, the mature-market equity risk premium and the country risk premium, with the beta multiplying both premia and the unlevered beta of 0.60 relevered to 0.76 at the company's market gearing — and a pre-tax cost of debt of 6.9% at a 25.7% debt weight, which is the US dollar risk-free rate plus the house corporate spread [S0]. That cost of debt is the forward marginal rate, not the 4.5% we carry in the P&L: the difference is about half a point of WACC, we keep the marginal rate because it is what a new issue would cost, and the financial section shows why the company can avoid paying it by retiring the 2028 bond from cash. We have not added a company-specific premium on top, although the single-buyer concentration [S3] would justify one; the sensitivity table shows what a percentage point does.

The DCF gives Rp1,225 per share and an enterprise value of 2,877.7 [S0]. The terminal value is 28.2% of that, normal for a utility with a twenty-year contracted horizon. Two choices drive the answer and we want them explicit, because they are the first thing a reader should be able to rebuild.

First, capex. The model spends 113.2 in FY2026E (24.0% of revenue), then 184.6 (38.0%) and 185.0 (34.0%) at the peak of the build; capex then runs at 32.0% of revenue in FY2029E and 34.0% in FY2030E before the step down. The build-up is bottom-up, not a percentage: over FY2026E-FY2028E the three years total about half a billion dollars, which is the remaining slice of Hululais's 435 USD m (about 110 MW at the project's own unit cost) plus the binary and low-pressure units in the public expose at that unit cost [S3,S5]. That is the path the model runs, and it is why the capex ratios in the table are what they are. From FY2031E the revenue path grows at the terminal rate of 2.0% a year and books no new capacity, so capex returns to the steady state that rate requires: the terminal depreciation ratio of 26.0% of revenue [S3], grossed up for the bull's terminal growth, which is 26.8% of revenue, down from the 34.0% of FY2030E. The terminal ratio is not the FY2025 audited charge of 126.9 on revenue of 432.7 [S3], which is a snapshot of a book still absorbing reclassifications from assets under construction; it applies the audited depreciation rate on the depreciable gross cost of 2,561 USD m [S3] to the gross cost after the committed build, which supports the 26.0% terminal ratio we use, marginally below the calculation. That is the capex that holds a constant real asset base and funds that growth; charging more than a third of revenue forever, as we did before this revision, would take about a fifth off the DCF — the single largest number in the model — and charging less than depreciation would mean a shrinking asset base. The company's ambition to reach 1,800 MW by 2034 [S4] is not in the revenue path in any scenario, so its capex is not charged in any scenario: it is an option we do not value. The sensitivity grid below runs WACC against terminal growth and revenue growth against gross margin, not capex, so the capex sensitivity is stated where it can be checked — in the line above, and in the bear case, which applies a fifth overrun to this path.

Second, the contracts end before the perpetuity does. Salak's contracts expire on 30 November 2040, Kamojang's on 31 December 2040 and Ulubelu's in 2041 [S3]. We model that explicitly: revenue growth holds at 2.0% from FY2031E, edges to 3.0% in FY2039E and 2.0% in FY2040E, then resets by -8.0% as the fleet re-contracts at the regulated ceiling rather than the legacy tariff. The terminal growth rate of 2.0% is therefore not contracted growth — it assumes renewal on similar terms after the reset, with terminal capex funding replacement wells. Non-renewal, or a harsher ceiling, is the bear case's terminal-growth shock.

The cross-checks disagree with the primary and with each other, and the reasons instruct. The peer EV/EBITDA benchmark is 19.5 times, worth Rp2,775 per share on our restated EBITDA. That median is three names and it is effectively one: BREN at about thirty-one times, KEEN at nineteen and a half (the median) and POWR at four and a half, a seven-to-one spread [S0]. None of the three peers' EV/EBITDA is restated on the audited-depreciation basis we had to apply to PGEO, and the same feed that carries a depreciation charge of about a million dollars for PGEO's 2,003.8 million asset base can distort a peer by the same defect, so a median set by one mid-cap geothermal name is not a fair-value benchmark. The dividend-yield cross-check gives Rp2,825 per share, built from a peer median yield of about one percent and PGEO's own average since listing — a listed history of roughly three and a half years and four dividends, not a five-year average — applied to a company yielding 7.1% [S0,S3]. We weight the two at 4.0% and 2.0%.

That is a deliberate departure from the house POWER_UTILITIES default weights, and the size of it should be stated rather than buried: at the card weights the blend would be six tenths of Rp1,225, three tenths of Rp2,775 and one tenth of Rp2,825, or roughly half again our DCF and about a third above our target, because three tenths of a default-weighted target would rest on the 19.5 times median we have just shown to be one name measured on an unrestated feed. We keep 94.0% of the target on the DCF and disclose the divergence; the honest reading is that PGEO screens cheap against a sector that is itself expensive on EBITDA multiples, and that the DCF, not the multiple, is the number to use.

The AFFO test from the method card, on one period at a time so the arithmetic cannot be flattered by the mix: FY2026E EBITDA of 382.4, less FY2026E capex of 113.2, less cash interest of 33.9 and cash tax of 72.9, measured against today's market capitalisation plus net debt of about thirty-five million dollars at 30 September 2026 [S0]. That yield is a fraction of a point below the ten-year rupiah sovereign of 7.45% — not above it. On the last audited year, FY2025, with the accrual capex addition of 102 USD m and that year's interest and tax, it is lower still, because EBITDA has not yet grown into the build; and it falls further in FY2027E and FY2028E, when capex rises to 184.6 and 185.0 at the peak of the programme. There is no consistent-period reading under which the cash yield clears the sovereign. The only version that appears to is the one in our first draft, which paired FY2026E EBITDA with FY2025 capex; it was wrong, and we withdraw it.

The card's rule is that infrastructure yielding less than the sovereign is duration risk wearing an equity costume, and by that rule PGEO fails. We record the failure rather than argue it away. What the rule does not do is price a contracted cash flow that runs to 2040-41, and that is what the DCF buys: Rp1,225 on the primary method against Rp930 [S0]. The mitigation is real but modest — net debt of about thirty-five million dollars against 382.4 of EBITDA means the leverage the spread is meant to pay for is almost absent — and it does not turn a miss into a pass. The dividend leg does not rescue it either: the shares yield 7.08% on our forecast against the same 7.45% sovereign, about a third of a point below, and the FY2027E forecast of 7.42% is still below it [S0]. So neither income leg of the card clears, and the rating is a discounted-cash-flow rating, with the cash-yield case explicitly not made and the shortfall disclosed here rather than used to justify it.

The card's output contract also asks for EV/EBITDA against the company's own history. We can give the current restated multiple — 6.6x on FY2025 EBITDA and 5.5x on FY2026E, both at today's price — but not a usable history: every earlier year in the data pack carries the same depreciation defect the restatement fixes [S3], so a series drawn from the feed would compare restated years with unrestated ones and flatter the past. What the current multiple says is enough for the cross-check: the shares change hands at a mid-single-digit multiple of an EBITDA that behaves like an annuity, and the 19.5x peer median is not a benchmark we will lean on.

We should be explicit about what this initiation keeps and drops from the idea card of October 2026 that we discarded, because two of its three objections still matter in a different form. The multiple objection is gone: the card saw a multiple above fifteen times because the data pack's EBITDA omitted most of a 126.9 depreciation charge, and on the audited charge the same price is the mid-single-digit multiple above [S3]. The AFFO objection is narrowed but not gone: more than a point short then, a fraction of a point short now, and still short, as the paragraph above sets out. The third objection — a share price at a premium to book on a return on equity under seven per cent — is the one the currency choice answers, and it deserves the arithmetic rather than a footnote.

PGEO earns dollars. The accounts are presented in dollars and the tariffs are dollar-linked [S3], and the model discounts those cash flows at a 10.0% dollar cost of equity — the US risk-free rate of 4.9%, a mature-market premium and an Indonesia country premium [S0]. Applying a rupiah cost of equity of eleven to thirteen per cent to the same cash flows double-counts the rupiah premium, because the forward exchange rate already carries the rate differential: the share price is quoted in rupiah, the cash flow is not. At our dollar cost of equity the card's own identity — justified price-to-book as return on equity less growth, over cost of equity less growth — gives about six-tenths of book on a return under seven per cent, not the four-tenths the card computed. The gap that remains to the DCF's Rp1,225 is the return-on-equity path: today's return is a trough, depressed by 718.5 of cash against 2,046.0 of equity and by 626 USD m of assets under construction that earn nothing until Hululais, at 87.8% complete, and the binary units come on line [S3]. Our model takes the return on equity to about ten per cent by FY2031E; if it stays where it is and the build earns nothing, the card is right and the value falls toward book, which is where our bear case sits (Rp832). The DCF implies about one and four-tenths times today's book and the target about one and a half, and that is the multiple to argue with.

The sensitivity grid is the honest range: a percentage point on the WACC moves the DCF by roughly a tenth, and the grid spans from about a sixth below the central DCF at the highest discount rate and lowest terminal growth to about a quarter above it at the other corner. No corner of the DCF grid falls below today's price of Rp930 [S0]: even a point higher on the WACC and a point lower on terminal growth leaves the shares trading under the modelled value. The twelve-month grid beneath it is less forgiving, because it moves the operating line and holds the discount rate and the capex path: with revenue growth four points a year slower and the gross margin a couple of points lower, the twelve-month value falls about five per cent under the last price, and the rest of that slowest-growth column sits within a few per cent of it rather than comfortably above. That, rather than the point estimate, is the basis of the rating — with one caveat neither grid can show, because both hold capex at our path: capex, not the discount rate, is the variable that would break the valuation, and the bear case applies a fifth overrun to it.

What the price implies. The reverse DCF is solved on our own model — the same cash flows and WACC, with a single uniform adjustment to revenue growth until the DCF equals the market price, so it is a model output rather than a citation. It says today's price discounts revenue growth of about 0.7% a year from FY2027E against the 3.0% we forecast. That is not a growth premium being withheld; a rate below the long-run inflation assumption assumes the contracted cash flow shrinks in real terms over contracts that run to 2040-41 [S3]. We cannot reconcile that with take-or-pay terms and a fleet that just produced a record nine months [S5]. It is, though, what a market that has fallen more than two-fifths since the end of 2025 will price [S10], and it is why we can call the shares cheap without claiming the growth plan is credible: the base case includes the twelve priority projects to the 1,047 MW installed by 2028 and excludes only the 1,800 MW ambition beyond it.

The target price of Rp1,395 is built in three steps from the DCF: the blend of 94.0% DCF, 4.0% EV/EBITDA and 2.0% dividend yield, worth Rp1,319, rolled forward at the cost of equity net of the next twelve months' dividend to Rp1,385, then weighted across the three scenarios to Rp1,395. It sits above the DCF for three disclosed reasons — the residual weight on the two cross-checks, the roll-forward, and the bull case carrying a quarter of the probability mass — and the bridge between the DCF and the target is therefore small and fully traceable: a DCF at Rp1,225, the weights above, and two cross-checks we do not trust enough to lean on.

Regulatory risk (high likelihood, high impact). The tariff under Perpres 112/2022 governs the return on every new megawatt and management is publicly lobbying for a revision [S4,S7]. A revision that goes the wrong way, or none at all, keeps new projects at a return close to the cost of capital and caps the growth option. The installed base is protected by signed contracts [S3], so this is a growth risk rather than a solvency risk.

Construction and delivery risk (high likelihood, medium impact). Hululais has been in construction for years and is only now approaching commercial operation with 2028 as the estimate [S3]. Geothermal projects slip on drilling results, permitting and grid connection, and the twelve priority projects each carry that risk. Our base case already phases them rather than delivering the 2028 target in full.

Counterparty and offtake risk (low likelihood, high impact). Almost all revenue comes from PLN group companies [S3]. PLN is state-owned and the contracts carry take-or-pay protection, so the realistic risk is payment timing rather than default, but a single buyer is a single buyer.

Commodity and currency (medium likelihood, medium impact). Revenue is dollar-linked and costs are partly rupiah, so a weaker rupiah helps at the margin; the risk is the reverse plus the translation of a dollar business into a rupiah share price [S0,S3]. There is no fuel exposure.

Refinancing (medium likelihood, medium impact). The green bond of 400 USD m matures in April 2028 [S3]. Refinancing at a higher coupon is the marginal cost our WACC carries, but the company holds enough cash to retire the bond [S5], so the realistic risk is a disorderly market rather than a forced refinancing.

Contract expiry (low likelihood before 2040, high impact). Salak, Kamojang and Ulubelu expire between November 2040 and 2041 [S3]. Our base case assumes renewal at the regulated ceiling and takes an explicit revenue reset in FY2041E; a non-renewal or a handover of the assets to the state would remove the terminal value the perpetuity assumes, which is the bear case's terminal-growth shock.

Dilution and index flow (medium likelihood, medium impact). The free-float commitment — 12.5% by March 2027 and 15.0% by 2028 [S4] — can be met by a divestment or a new share issue, and the two have opposite effects on per-share value; management has also ruled out a buyback because it would shrink the float [S4]. Separately, the MSCI review of Indonesia's market classification is a flow event for the whole market, not just PGEO, and the company was asked about it in November [S10]. The bear case carries the issue at four per cent of shares; the index event we leave to the market-risk section rather than double-count inside the equity.

Governance and liquidity (medium likelihood, medium impact). With a free float of 11.2% [S4] the shares are exposed to flow events: the planned increase to 12.5% in March 2027 could be a divestment or a new issue, and the two have opposite effects on per-share value [S4]. Thin liquidity also means the shares can overshoot on index news that says nothing about the assets, which is part of what the current discount reflects [S10].
Tax and fiscal (low likelihood, medium impact). The effective rate has run near thirty percent [S3]; a change to geothermal fiscal treatment in either direction would move the DCF.

Scenarios. We shock four drivers: revenue growth by three percentage points each way, terminal growth by a point each way, and share count, where the bear takes a four per cent new issue and the bull takes none, because the free-float target can be met by the controlling shareholder's sell-down instead [S4]. The fourth is capex intensity, which the bear raises by a fifth; the bull carries no capex saving, because a permanent cut would also cut terminal replacement capex below depreciation and shrink the asset base. The brownfield unit-cost saving [S5] is therefore a qualitative upside, not a modelled one. The base case keeps the largest share of the probability mass and the bear almost a third, up from a quarter, because the bear now carries the channels the company itself discloses — a capex overrun, dilution and a weaker renewal at the 2039-41 expiries.

In the bear case Hululais slips a further year past 2028, the project overruns by a fifth, the free-float requirement is met with a four per cent new issue at a fifteen per cent discount (the engine takes the share count; the discount is worth a further fraction of a percent of per-share value on top), and the 2039-41 contracts are renewed on worse terms so terminal growth falls to a point. Revenue grows three points a year slower than base and the dividend cover is stretched. That gives Rp832. In the bull case the tariff revision lands, the Kamojang data-centre offtake opens private tariffs above the regulated ceiling, the twelve projects execute on schedule, with the brownfield unit-cost saving a qualitative upside not in the capex line, and the same three points of growth and a point more terminal growth: Rp2,088. The base case gives Rp1,385. The valuation is asymmetric because the starting price is Rp930 and the base case is worth Rp1,385; we are not relying on the bull case to justify the rating. Two things should be said plainly about the distribution. The bear is only about a tenth below the current price, and that is the point rather than a weakness: at today's level the market is already close to our downside case, so the asymmetry sits in the base and the bull, not in a bear that has further to fall. The bull carries no capex saving, so it is if anything conservative: the brownfield unit-cost saving is not in the numbers.

Signposts that would change our view. An upward revision of the geothermal tariff ceiling under Perpres 112/2022 would raise the value of the growth option and push us towards the bull case. A credible plan to fund the build without diluting at these prices, or evidence that project returns clear the cost of capital by a wide margin, would do the same. On the other side, a further slip in Hululais beyond 2028, a dividend cut below the stated floor, or a new share issue at a deep discount to fund capex would move us towards the bear case; so would a sustained rise in the US dollar rate path that lifts the cost of capital by more than a point.

Ownership and control. PGEO is controlled by PT Pertamina Power Indonesia within the Pertamina group; the free float is 11.2% and the balance of the register is the group's, with institutional holders outside it a small share of a thin market [S4]. The insider figure carried by the market-data feed is inconsistent with the audited float and overstates the group's stake; we use the free-float disclosure. The state's strategic interest in geothermal is why the company exists in its current form and explains both the growth ambition and the tariff lobbying [S4,S7]. Minority holders should expect the company to be run in the national interest where that conflicts with per-share value; the free-float commitment is the main counterweight and management frames it as a regulatory obligation rather than a choice [S4].

Related parties. The dominant related party is PLN, which buys the steam and electricity: a commercial relationship at regulated prices rather than a value-transfer channel, but it means almost all revenue is transacted with a party related through the state [S3]. Related-party receivables and payables are disclosed and small relative to revenue [S3]. There are joint operating contracts with international partners where PGEO acts as principal in some fields and as an intermediary in others [S3]; those structures deserve monitoring because the accounting margin depends on the contractual role.

Pledged shares and structure. We found no disclosure of pledged controlling shares in the audited accounts [S3]. There has been no serial rights issue: the share count has moved only slightly through employee programmes [S3]. The risk to watch is the reverse, a new share issue to raise the free float, which is one of the options management has flagged [S4].

Audit and accounts. The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja of the Ernst & Young network, with an unmodified opinion and a key audit matter on the impairment of fixed assets, the right area to test given that fixed assets are the bulk of the balance sheet [S3]. The accounts are in US dollars, which removes translation noise from the operating lines but not from the share price.

Dividend record and policy. The company declared 124 USD m on FY2025 earnings at a payout ratio of 89.9% [S2], having distributed a similar proportion the year before [S0]. The prospectus policy is a ceiling of fifty percent, exceeded each year with shareholder approval [S2]. We treat the high payout as a feature of the case with a caveat: it is sustainable only while capex is modest, and capex is about to rise.

Board and ESG exposures. Geothermal carries a specific set of environmental and social issues: drilling in volcanic terrain, water and steam management, land acquisition and community relations in rural areas, and the reputational risk of operating near protected forest. Company disclosures emphasise baseload decarbonisation, local content and community programmes, and it has received environment-related recognition [S7]. The material ESG risk for an investor is not the operating footprint but the licence to build: social acceptance and permitting set the pace of the pipeline, and the company itself lists synchronisation of working areas, the grid plan and power purchase agreements as the binding constraints [S7].

The dated catalysts are in the frontmatter. The ones we would trade are these. The FY2026 audited results in the first quarter of 2027 will show whether the 2026 margin holds once the fourth-quarter depreciation true-up lands, and the dividend declaration alongside them tests whether management can hold a payout above half of earnings while capex rises. The free-float increase to 12.5% in March 2027 is a flow event whose direction depends on whether it is a divestment or an issue [S4]. The first priority-project units reaching commercial operation are the initial test of whether the twelve-project programme can deliver on schedule [S5], and Hululais in 2028 is the largest single step. The tariff revision is undated and cannot be scheduled, but it is the largest swing factor in the bull case [S4].

Between updates we monitor a short list. Production in gigawatt hours against the 2026 record run-rate [S5]. Availability and forced outage rate, because a baseload annuity is worth what its uptime is worth [S5]. Realised revenue per megawatt hour, which is the tariff by another name and what the Perpres review would change. Capex as a share of revenue against our build assumption, because that is the variable that moves the DCF most. Net debt and the refinancing of the 2028 bond [S3]. And the free-float path against the stated commitments [S4].

The listed Indonesian geothermal universe is small and the state dominates it. That has two practical consequences for a minority investor: liquidity is thin, so position sizing matters as much as the view, and the controlling shareholder's national-energy agenda will sometimes override the commercial optimum. Both are reasons to demand a valuation discount, not reasons to avoid the asset class.

sensitivity.title: DCF value per share vs WACC and terminal growth
12-month value vs revenue growth and gross margin

assumptions.label: Revenue growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E +9.0%: 9M2026 revenue of US$352.2m (+10.46% yoy [S4,S5]) annualises to about US$472m against US$432.7m in FY2025 [S3] once the fourth quarter is grown only about 5%, because Q4 2025 was already the first full quarter with Lumut Balai Unit 2 (55 MW, operating certificate 29 June 2025 [S3]). FY2027E +3.0% comes from the capacity bridge alone: about 2pp of remaining Lumut Balai Unit 2 annualisation and 1pp from the first binary/low-pressure units with 2027 target COD [S5]. The LK discloses no tariff escalator in the PPA note [S3], so none is added. FY2028E +12.0% is Hululais Units 1 and 2 (110 MW, US$435m, COD 2028 [S3,F25]) at a partial year plus the binary units; FY2029E +8.0% and FY2030E +4.0% phase the rest of the 12 priority projects [S5]. FY2031E to FY2038E hold 2.0% a year: the base books no capacity after the twelve priority projects and the LK discloses no tariff escalator in the PPA note [S3], so growth is inflation-level only. FY2039E +3.0%, FY2040E +2.0% and an 8% one-off reset in FY2041E mark the expiry of the Salak (30 November 2040), Kamojang (31 December 2040) and Ulubelu (2041) contracts [S3]: we assume renewal at the regulated ceiling, which is a lower tariff than the legacy contracts. Long run 2.0% thereafter.

assumptions.label: Gross margin at base input costs
assumptions.basis: Derived, not disclosed: the 9M2026 release gives revenue US$352.2m and company-reported EBITDA US$287.77m [S5] but no cost-of-revenue line. We derive cost of revenue including depreciation as revenue less EBITDA less G&A of US$20.0m [S4] plus our 9M D&A estimate of about US$104m (three quarters of the FY2025 audited US$126.9m charge [S3]), i.e. US$352.2m - US$287.77m - US$20.0m + US$104m = about US$148m, or 57.8% of revenue. The audited FY2025 gross margin was 53.86% [S3]; the step up is Lumut Balai Unit 2 running a full year against a largely fixed cost base, and it holds through FY2030E because no new cost layer is added before Hululais.

assumptions.label: SG&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: General and administrative expense fell 15.03% to US$20m in 9M2026 [S4], about 5.7% of revenue and below the FY2025 audited US$30.7m (7.1% of revenue) [S3]; held at 5.7% rather than the 6.55% three-year average because the reduction is already in the reported numbers.

assumptions.label: D&A / revenue
assumptions.basis: Restated from the audited note: depreciation charged in cost of revenue was US$126.9m in FY2025 and US$112.3m in FY2024 [S3], against a data pack that carries US$1.0m. FY2026E US$136m is the 9M2026 charge implied by the reported EBITDA of US$287.77m [S5] plus the normal fourth-quarter depreciation true-up. The terminal ratio is an asset-base calculation, not the FY2025 ratio: the audited FY2025 charge of US$126.9m is 29.3% of revenue (FY2024 27.6%) [S3], a snapshot of a book still absorbing the 2024-25 reclassifications from assets under construction rather than a steady-state ratio. The fixed-asset note gives depreciable gross cost of US$2,538.6m (acquisition cost US$2,560.9m less land US$22.3m) and a FY2025 charge of US$126.2m, a 4.97% depreciation rate on gross cost [S3]. Cumulative capex of about US$878.6m over FY2026E-FY2030E lifts depreciable gross cost to about US$3,417m by FY2031E; 4.97% of that is about US$170m, or 26.7% of FY2031E revenue of US$635.6m. We hold 26.0% as the terminal assumption, marginally below the calculation, and label it as such rather than as the audited charge.

assumptions.label: Capex / revenue
assumptions.basis: The build while it lasts, then the steady state a 2% perpetuity needs. 9M2026 additions to fixed assets ran at about US$72m (quarterly data pack) so FY2026E lands near US$113m, 24% of revenue; FY2027E and FY2028E are about US$185m each (38% and 34%), which is the remaining 12% of Hululais's US$435m (about US$52m [S3,F26,F27]) plus 105 MW of binary and low-pressure units at the Hululais unit cost of US$3.95m/MW (US$435m / 110 MW), i.e. about US$415m [S3,S5]. FY2029E and FY2030E at 32-34% carry the rest of the twelve priority projects toward the 1,047 MW 2028 target and into 2030 [S4]. After FY2030E the revenue path grows 2% a year (the revenue_growth long-run rate) with no new capacity booked, so capex returns to the steady state a perpetuity requires: the terminal depreciation ratio of 26% of revenue (see the da_pct basis for the asset-base calculation) times (1 + 3%) = 26.8%. The 3% is the bull case's terminal growth, so no scenario runs capex below depreciation and shrinks the asset base; the base case's own 2% path is therefore charged 0.3pp of extra replacement capex, which is immaterial. The 1.8 GW by 2034 ambition [S4] is not in the revenue path in any scenario, so its capex is not charged in any scenario - it is an option we do not value. Charging more than depreciation forever would capitalise growth the base case never books; charging less would mean a shrinking asset base.

assumptions.label: Operating working capital / revenue
assumptions.basis: engine default: average of FY2023A, FY2024A, FY2025A (div(nwc, revenue))

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: FY2025 effective rate was 29.7% (tax US$58.2m on pre-tax profit US$195.9m) [S3]; held at 30% because the gap to the headline rate is small and stable.

assumptions.label: Cost of debt (P&L interest on opening debt)
assumptions.basis: This is the P&L rate on the existing book, not the WACC rate: FY2025 finance costs were US$30.3m on opening debt US$745.8m = 4.06% [S3], and the US$400m green bond carries a fixed 5.15% coupon to April 2028 [S3,F29]; we hold 4.5%. The WACC uses a separate forward marginal cost of debt of 6.86% (4.86% USD risk-free plus a 2.0% corporate spread), because new borrowing would be priced there. The gap matters only while the existing fixed-rate book is in place: with US$713.7m of cash at 30 Sep 2026 against US$752.9m of debt [S5] the group can repay the 2028 bond without refinancing, so the marginal rate is an option the company need not exercise.

assumptions.label: Yield on opening cash
assumptions.basis: finance income US$28.2m on opening cash US$655.2m = 4.31% in FY2025 [S3]; held there.

assumptions.label: Net new borrowing
assumptions.basis: No new net debt: operating cash flow (about US$380m at the FY2026E EBITDA) covers capex of US$110-150m and the dividend, and the balance sheet already holds US$713.7m of cash at 30 Sep 2026 against US$752.9m of debt [S3,S5].

assumptions.label: Other non-operating items
assumptions.basis: Includes the FX loss and joint-venture share that sit below operating profit in the audited accounts; FY2025 net was a US$7.6m FX loss and US$0.04m JV profit [S3], so a flat zero neutral assumption is the most likely central case.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: Minority interest is US$0.03m of a US$137.7m profit in FY2025 [S3] — PGE consolidates wholly owned operating entities; held at zero.

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Held at the FY2025 actual of 89.9% (US$123.9m declared) [S2,F20], because the company has reopened the possibility of paying above the 50% prospectus ceiling for FY2026 [S2] and the cash flow covers it: FY2025 audited operating cash flow of US$313.5m less capex of US$84.4m less dividends of US$136.4m still left about US$93m [S3], and at our FY2026E EBITDA the same arithmetic stays positive through the FY2027E-FY2028E capex peak. Payout is not treated as a fixed policy: a capex overrun that breaks that cover is the bear case's dividend channel.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: No buyback (management ruled it out to protect free float [S4]); any free-float increase to 12.5% by March 2027 or 15% in 2028 is described as a divestment or a new share issue, so a fully dilutive assumption is not the base case until an option is chosen [S4].

assumptions.label: Terminal growth (DCF)
assumptions.basis: House terminal growth for a USD reporter, applied after the FY2041E re-contracting reset. The operating PPAs expire between November 2040 and 2041 (Salak 30 November 2040, Kamojang 31 December 2040, Ulubelu 2041 [S3]), so 2% is not contracted growth: it assumes the working areas are renewed at the regulated Perpres 112/2022 ceiling on similar terms, that the 8% reset already taken in FY2041E stands, and that terminal capex above depreciation continues to fund replacement wells. A non-renewal or a harsher ceiling is the bear case's terminal-growth shock.

challenges.challenge: Capex, which the report calls its first value driver, is described in assumptions as 'FY2027E-FY2028E rise to about US$150m a year' and in section 4 as 'about a third of revenue', but the model runs 191.8 (38% of revenue) and 188.8 (34%). The gap is about US$40m a year, roughly 8pp of revenue, which on the report's own 10%-per-few-points statement is 15-20% of the DCF. A reader cannot reproduce the number the thesis depends on.
challenges.answer: Restated the capex basis to the path the model runs: about 184.6 and 185.0 in FY2027E-FY2028E, built bottom-up from the remaining Hululais spend plus the binary units at the project unit cost [S3,S5]. The US$150m claim is gone, the prose carries the modelled placeholders, and the capex +20% case is now an explicit scenario shock.

challenges.challenge: The engine's WACC uses a 6.86% pre-tax cost of debt (kd_pre_tax 0.06859) while assumptions set cost_of_debt at 4.5% and the audited FY2025 effective rate is 4.06% (US$30.3m on opening debt US$745.8m, S3). Two of the model's own inputs disagree by 2.4pp on a 25.8% debt weight, worth about 0.6pp of WACC and ~6% of the DCF, and the disclosure in section 4 mentions rf, ERP, CRP and beta but never the cost of debt or the debt weight.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now states the pre-tax cost of debt of 6.9% and the 25.8% debt weight, and reconciles them with the 4.5% carried in the P&L: the WACC uses the forward marginal rate (US risk-free plus the house spread), the P&L the legacy effective 4.1% to 5.15% book [S3]. Section 3 adds that the 2028 bond can be repaid from cash, so the marginal rate is optional.

challenges.challenge: The target rests 94% on the DCF, against the house POWER_UTILITIES default of 60/30/10. The report explains why it distrusts the peer sample but never quantifies the choice for the reader: at the default weights the target would be roughly 0.6x1,139 + 0.3x2,782 + 0.1x2,212 = about Rp1,740, some 28% above the Rp1,226 blend used. The QC weights.changed WARN is left unjustified.
challenges.answer: Section 4 now quantifies the divergence: at the house default weights the blend would be about two-fifths above our DCF because three tenths would rest on a peer median that is one name measured on an unrestated feed [S0,S3]. We keep 94% on the DCF, disclose the counterfactual and answer the weights.changed WARN in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Payout is cut to 70% from an 89.9% actual (US$123.9m, S2) on the argument that capex competes for the same cash. The only company statement on record is that a payout above the 50% prospectus cap is being opened up again for FY2026 (S2), and cash flow covers it: OCF 313.5 less capex 84.4 less dividends 136.4 leaves ~93m in FY2025. The cut lowers both the div-yield cross-check and the DPS subtracted in the target roll-forward (52 vs ~66 at the actual ratio).
challenges.answer: Payout held at the FY2025 actual of 89.9% rather than cut to 70%, sourced to the company reopening a distribution above half of earnings for FY2026 [S2]; the cover arithmetic uses the audited operating cash flow, capex and dividends [S3] and the capex-overrun dividend channel is the bear case.

challenges.challenge: Revenue growth is set at 9.0% for FY2026E against a reported 10.46% for 9M2026 (S5) and 7.0% for FY2027E, with the FY2027E step attributed to 'tariff escalation' whose rate, index and source are never given. The LK does not disclose an escalator, so the growth path that drives the whole DCF cannot be checked. On the model's own sensitivity, +1pp of growth is worth roughly 8% of value.
challenges.answer: Removed the unsourced tariff-escalation claim: the LK discloses no escalator [S3], so the path is the capacity bridge alone, FY2027E growth of 3% being the residual annualisation of Lumut Balai 2 plus the first binary units with 2027 COD [S5]. FY2026E of 9.0% is explained as the annualisation of a 9M rate of 10.5% against a high fourth-quarter base.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 asserts that holding the gross margin at the 2026 run-rate 'means none of our EBITDA improvement comes from margin expansion'. It does: EBITDA margin runs 76.8% in FY2025A and 81.1% in FY2026E, the 4.23pp calibration gap, because D&A falls as a share of revenue even with a flat gross margin. The prose tells the reader the opposite of what the model does, and that is the wrong side of the ledger to be vague about in an initiation whose thesis is that the market underrates the margin.
challenges.answer: Rewrote the margin passage: the model expands the EBITDA margin from 76.8% to 81.1% and the report now says so, sourced to Lumut Balai 2 running a full year plus the 15% G&A reduction [S3,S4]. The 4.2pp calibration gap is answered in qc_justifications.

challenges.challenge: Section 3 says 'operating cash flow was 184.1 in FY2025 on our restated definition against capex of 84.4'. The 184.1 is the model's fcff, which is already net of the 84.4 capex and 58.2 tax (EBITDA 332.5 less tax less capex less working capital). The audited operating cash flow is 313.5 (S3 cash flow). The sentence both understates OCF by 130m and double-counts capex by comparing a post-capex number to the capex line.
challenges.answer: Replaced the fcff figure in the cash-flow sentence with a new fact for the audited operating cash flow of 313.5 (F36, S3), and labelled the 184.1 explicitly as free cash flow to the firm, the number the DCF discounts, no longer compared with capex.

challenges.challenge: Three citations do not support what they are attached to: (i) the reverse DCF result of 5.3% growth is cited to [S4], a news article that says nothing about a reverse DCF; (ii) the 57.85% gross margin and the 9M2026 'cost of revenue US$148.7m' appear in no archived source, they are back-solved from the reported US$287.77m EBITDA and US$20m opex; (iii) the dividend-yield cross-check rests on PGEO's 'five-year average' yield when the price history begins February 2023. In addition there is no valuation.post_bs_review entry, which the base-case card requires.
challenges.answer: Reverse DCF now attributed to our model rather than a news source; the gross margin labelled derived with the arithmetic shown and sourced to the 9M release and audited D&A [S3,S5]; dividend-yield history corrected to the listing period and four dividends; valuation.post_bs_review added naming the sources searched since 30 September 2026.

challenges.challenge: The bear case bears almost no weight: it shocks only revenue growth and gross margin, and lands at Rp915, 1.6% below a price that has already fallen with a 43% IHSG drawdown (S10). It omits the three downside channels the report itself raises: a Hululais or binary-unit capex overrun (the project has been in build for years, its shareholders' agreement and PPA were still being finalised in November 2026, S5), dilution or an overhang from the free-float increase to 15% by 2028 through a possible new share issue (S4), and an MSCI standalone reclassification (S10). A bear case that says the downside is 2% needs to be stress-tested on the lever the report calls its biggest.
